title: Scale + Ouster Partnership

reason: Read in full: a 2-min business post announcing a data-format integration between Ouster's LiDAR output and Scale's annotation pipeline; the only substantive claims are product benefits ("streamlined data transfer", "no sensor fusion required") and a forward-looking intent to sign more sensor partnerships. Nothing is measured and no AI system is assessed.

title: nuScenes
rule_cited: §2 test 2 — dataset release announcement; counts describe the artefact, not an assessed system
reason: Read in full: Scale announces the full release of Aptiv's nuScenes AV dataset for which it was the labelling partner. The numbers present (1.4M camera images, 390k LiDAR sweeps, "7x more object annotations than KITTI") are dataset inventory and a comparator statistic, not a result from evaluating any model; the rest is aspiration ("we hope to do for the autonomous vehicle community what ImageNet did for computer vision").

reason: Read in full: a 1-min launch post for Scale's Sensor Fusion Segmentation annotation endpoint. reason: Read in full: $100M Series C at a >$1B valuation, investor list, and an essay on the training-data bottleneck. Assertions such as "safe, accurate and unbiased AI systems depend on large volumes of high quality training data" are position statements, not measured findings.

reason: Read in full: Scale notes its selection to the Forbes AI 50 list and links its Series C and a LinkedIn Top Startups listing. No AI system is examined.

title: Open-Source Dataset for Wintry Conditions
rule_cited: §2 test 2 — dataset release announcement; the measured work sits in a separate paper by other authors (also §3 duplicate/secondary)
reason: Read in full: Scale, Waterloo and Toronto open-source the Canadian Adverse Driving Conditions (CADC) dataset — 7,000 LiDAR/camera frames over 70 sequences from 20 km of snowy Ontario driving, with Scale providing annotations. The claims about snow degrading AV perception are stated as general background, not measured here; the post itself points to a separate arXiv paper by the Waterloo/Toronto researchers for the technical characterisation, so this page is secondary even if that paper were in scope.

title: A Survey of Deep Learning Approaches for OCR and Document Understanding
rule_cited: §2 test 1 — an explicit survey consolidating other researchers' methods, not claims asserted by the evaluator
reason: Read the Scale Labs landing page and abstract in full (NeurIPS 2020 ML-RSA workshop, Subramani/Matton/Greaves/Lam). The paper's stated purpose is to "review different techniques for document understanding" and "consolidate methodologies present in literature to act as a jumping-off point for researchers" — by construction a summary of others' work, with no result of its own. Also §4b: the subject matter is OCR/document-understanding accuracy.

title: Series D
rule_cited: §2 test 2 — funding, product and acquisition announcement, no measured result
reason: Read in full: $155M Series D at >$3.5B led by Tiger Global, the Nucleus product launch and the Helia AI acquisition, plus a customer list. Business facts about the company, not findings about an AI system.

title: Series E
rule_cited: §2 test 2 + §1 company self-report — vendor performance claims about Scale's own service, no external evaluator
reason: Read in full: $325M Series E. It does carry numbers a keyword filter might flag — Scale "improve[d] Toyota's annotation throughput by 10X" and raised States Title's document-processing accuracy "to more than 95 percent" — but these are self-asserted marketing metrics about Scale's own commercial pipeline with no external evaluator and no method, and document-processing accuracy is out of scope under §4b in any case.

title: On The State of Data In Computer Vision: Human Annotations Remain Indispensable for Developing Deep Learning Models
rule_cited: §2 test 1 — a survey of other groups' results; its conclusion is a synthesis, not an evaluator-asserted measurement
reason: Read the Scale Labs page and abstract in full (Emam et al., Scale AI + University of Maryland). The paper explicitly says "we survey computer vision research domains" and "summarize the community's current understanding"; the headline conclusion that non-synthetic labelled data "remains indispensable" is drawn from the surveyed literature, not from an evaluation the authors ran.

title: DEBAGREEMENT: A comment-reply dataset for (dis)agreement detection in online debates
date_source: Scale Labs page date stamp ("10/11/2021"); paper is NeurIPS 2021 Datasets & Benchmarks Track (Round 2)
rule_cited: §2 — evaluator-asserted, evidence-backed, independently codeable methodology finding (§2 expressly admits methodology and tooling findings); §4 Gate 1 no → Tier C
reason: THE FILTER LOST THIS ONE. The title is a dataset name with no evaluation keyword, so both the title triage and the keyword rule dropped it — but the landing page is filed by Scale itself under "Safety & Oversight / Evaluation and Alignment", and the full paper (recovered via the Wayback id_ route to the OpenReview PDF after openreview.net served a browser-check shell) contains a genuine, measured evaluation-methodology result: models fine-tuned on the clean, formal Perspectrum stance corpus transfer so badly to messy online debate data that they fall below the majority-class baseline on two of five subreddits. Scale AI + University of Oxford are external to the developers of the models tested (BERT, RoBERTa, DeBERTa, XLNet), so §1's self-report drop does not bite. The plain accuracy numbers (62-64%) are themselves out of scope under §4b; what is coded is the benchmark-validity claim, not the accuracy.

findings.finding: Language models fine-tuned on a clean, formal (dis)agreement corpus (Perspectrum) transfer poorly to messy social-media debate data: BERT base/uncased reaches 90.5% in-domain on Perspectrum but drops to 54-58% across the five DEBAGREEMENT subreddits, failing to beat the naive most-frequent-class baseline on r/BlackLivesMatter and r/climate — evidence that formal stance-detection benchmarks do not measure the online task they are assumed to proxy.
findings.finding_quote: BERT(b/u) trained on Perspectrum performs poorly on DEBAGREEMENT.
findings.models_systems: BERT (base/uncased) as the probe model; benchmark suite also covers BERT large/uncased, XLNet base/large, RoBERTa base/large, DeBERTa base/large
findings.domain: evaluation methodology / benchmark validity and domain transfer
findings.tier_reasoning: Gate 1: this is not an empirical finding about a model's capability or safety — the claim is about the datasets, specifically that a formal stance corpus is not a valid proxy for online (dis)agreement detection, with the language models serving as the instrument that demonstrates it. Gate 1 answers no, so eval_trackable is "no", action_trackable stays BLANK and the tier is C. (Had it been coded as a model finding it would still have failed Gate 2 condition (c): non-frontier 2018-2021 encoder models used as the instrument of a benchmark study, with ordinary classification accuracy as the metric.)
findings.scope: benchmark-level (cross-corpus transfer: Perspectrum vs DEBAGREEMENT, 42,894 Reddit comment-reply pairs across five subreddits)
findings.access_type: open weights (HuggingFace implementations fine-tuned locally on 2x NVIDIA TITAN RTX)

title: GlideNet: Global, Local and Intrinsic based Dense Embedding NETwork for Multi-category Attributes Prediction
rule_cited: §1 hard drop — developer reporting its own model's score with no external evaluator; §4b — ordinary benchmark accuracy
reason: Read the Scale Labs page and abstract in full. GlideNet is an architecture Scale AI proposed (with Penn State) and benchmarked itself on VAW and CAR, reporting ">5% gain over state of the art in the mean recall (mR) metric". The measured party and the measuring party are the same, no external evaluator is named, and the metric is ordinary attribute-prediction accuracy. This is a self-reported capability result, not an evaluation.

title: Ukraine Detection
rule_cited: §2 test 2 — dataset donation plus capability marketing; the "high-accuracy" claims are unquantified and self-asserted
reason: Read in full: Scale offers free AI-ready satellite-imagery datasets (aircraft detection, structure damage assessment, change detection) to national-security users after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. It describes challenges for its own change-detection models (weather, mixed image quality, rare objects such as TELs) and asserts it delivers "high-accuracy, time-sensitive insights", but reports no measurement, no method and no external evaluator — a capability advertisement for Scale's own deployed system.

title: Text: The Universal Interface
rule_cited: §2 test 2 — an opinion essay; every empirical claim in it is a link to someone else's work (§2 test 1 also fails)
reason: Read the full 13-min essay — the longest Scale item in this chunk (16k chars) and the one most likely to look promising, since it discusses GPT-2/GPT-3 behaviour, prompt sensitivity, personas and prompt-engineering "test sets". But nothing is measured by the author: the concrete claims (LLMs can play chess, "unreal engine" improving image generations, prompt phrasing changing arithmetic performance, models "hiding" capability behind a played character) are all hyperlinked to third-party posts and papers, and the piece's own contribution is the UNIX-pipe analogy. Not evidence-backed in this report.

title: Best 10 Public Datasets for Object Detection
rule_cited: §2 test 1 — a curated listing of third-party datasets; the numbers quoted are other groups' published results
reason: Read in full: a marketing listicle of ten public object-detection datasets (ImageNet, COCO, etc.) with size, licence and citation for each. Figures such as AlexNet's 16% ILSVRC top-5 error are recited from the original 2012 work, not produced or verified here.

rule_cited: §2 test 1 — a three-page review consolidating other researchers' systems; also §1, no DSRI/ULRI author or affiliation on the record
reason: IEEE Xplore serves a JS shell direct (870 chars of navigation), 202/404 through the rest of the ladder including Wayback, and a first DOI guess resolved to an unrelated CSCI 2022 paper; identity was finally pinned via Crossref bibliographic search. Record: DOI 10.1109/csci58124.2022.00329, pages 1827-1829, 25 references, authors Ryan Ackerman and Renu Balyan (SUNY Old Westbury) and Francisco Icobelli (Northeastern Illinois University), funded by NSF awards 2131052/2219586/2219587. Two independent grounds to exclude: it is a "Concise Review" of prior intelligent-tutoring-system work rather than an evaluation the authors ran, and nothing in the authorship, affiliations or funding ties it to DSRI/ULRI, so the venue attribution in the source list is not supported. The full abstract text could not be retrieved, so the exclusion rests on the title, the three-page review format and the authorship record rather than on the body text.
